original.source: Every number computed in the following chapters is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalisation are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action and the linear differential $Q$ [C07, §4.3]. The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase “natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure” [ESW, Def 1.34]. This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.

The ten-dimensional space is $V_{10}=V_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, where $V_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^{10}$ carries its Euclidean form and the orthogonal decomposition $V_{\mathbb R}=W_{\mathbb R}\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ of [ESW, §2.2, §2.6]: $W_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^4$ is spacetime and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions. With $V=W_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$,

and from here on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ denote these complexifications. The nondegenerate symmetric form $(-,-)$ of $V_{10}$ is the complex-bilinear extension of the Euclidean form. The letter $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

The gauge Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is complex, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$ [ESW, §3.1], chosen positive definite on the compact real form, so that $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is negative definite on the real slice of [C07, §6.6] (Remark [1.10](#b-00080)). The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$. The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

The map $q\colon\wedge^\bullet V_{10}\to\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ is antisymmetrisation, $q(v_1\wedge v_2)=v_1v_2-(v_1,v_2)$ [ESW, (29)]. Applied to a two-form, such as $F_A$, the symbol $\rho$ means $\rho\circ q$, as in $\rho(F_A)$ [ESW, (33)].

The exterior derivative $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and every field is constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume density of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator $\Gamma(\Sigma)\to\Gamma(\Sigma^*)$ [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.

Fix an orientation of $V$. For an oriented orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_4$ of $V$ the element $q(v_1\wedge v_2\wedge v_3\wedge v_4)=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ of $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ depends on the orientation alone. The operator $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$. Writing

The element $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ is the antisymmetrisation $q$ of the oriented unit element of $\wedge^4V$, hence depends on the orientation alone. By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence

Moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for each $v_i$, hence for every $v\in V$ by linearity. For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$. Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$. For the multiplicities, take a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$. ∎

The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them. This orientation is fixed once; Chapter 2 uses it to name the supercharges.

An affine function that vanishes at $-\tfrac14$ and is nonzero at $+\tfrac14$ has $-\tfrac14$ as its unique zero; in particular it is nonzero at $-\tfrac12$. ∎

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ fix bases of $\mathfrak g$, of $V_{10}$ and of $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ in which the bracket, the pairings, $\rho$ and $\Gamma$ have Gaussian-rational entries. The density of each local functional of this chapter, and of each bracket of two of them, is then a polynomial in the jets of the components of the six fields with Gaussian-rational coefficients, computed in exact arithmetic. A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D$ without constant term vanishes on $\mathscr E_c$ when all Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ vanish identically: for $e\in\mathscr E_c$, after integration by parts with compact support, $\frac{d}{ds}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is the integral of the Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ at $se$ paired with $e$ (odd components multiplied by odd elements of an auxiliary nilpotent ring, as in Definition [1.13](#b-00112)), so $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is independent of $s$ and equals its value $0$ at $s=0$. Conversely, a nonzero Euler–Lagrange derivative shows that the functional is nonzero. Statements that a bracket vanishes for every element of $\Sigma$ are established on every element of a basis of $\Sigma$; this suffices, because the bracket is linear in that element.

The dilatation of a composite operator, and every other superconformal transformation, acts on the fields of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory [ESW, Def 2.4, §10.3] up to gauge transformations and equations of motion. In the BV formalism this structure is a Maurer–Cartan element of a Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, an $L_\infty$ action in the sense of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27], and it is the classical input of the equivariant observables used later. [ESW, (32)–(34), Thm 3.3] construct it for the Poincaré supersymmetry algebra; the special conformal transformations and the special supercharges require Weyl weights, a compensating term with the six scalars, and an R-symmetry rotation in the odd bracket. This chapter realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, the complexification of $\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ [SW, (7)], on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, fixes the sign conventions of the complex, writes the action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, and proves its master equation for every gauge algebra.
